title: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation

topics.title: Harappan civilisation: names, culture and sites

learn.hook: Over 4,500 years ago, people from the Indus plains to Gujarat were using the same kind of bricks, seals and weights. How do we even name a world that left no readable writing?
points: The Indus valley civilisation is also called the Harappan civilisation, after Harappa, the first site where it was discovered.

In archaeology, a 'culture' means a group of objects of a distinctive style, usually found together within a specific geographical area and period of time. Harappan seals, beads, weights and stone blades form such a group.
The Mature Harappan phase is dated c. 2600–1900 BCE. Cultures before it in the same area are called Early Harappan; those after it are called Late Harappan.

Early Harappan settlements were generally small, had distinctive pottery, agriculture and pastoralism, and some crafts. A break between early and mature phases is shown by large-scale burning at some sites and abandonment of certain settlements.

Key sites: Harappa and Mohenjodaro (now in Pakistan), Dholavira and Lothal (Gujarat), Kalibangan (Rajasthan), Rakhigarhi and Banawali (Haryana), Chanhudaro (Sindh), Nageshwar (Gujarat coast), Balakot (Baluchistan coast) and Shortughai (Afghanistan).

example.q: A student finds burnt layers at a site lying between Early Harappan pottery below and Mature Harappan seals above. What does this suggest?
steps: Lower layers are older; upper layers are younger.
Early Harappan material lies below, so it came first.
Burnt layers between them point to destruction or a break.
This matches the break seen at some sites before the mature phase.
example.answer: There was a break, possibly with burning and abandonment, between the Early Harappan and Mature Harappan phases at that site.

learn.reallife: Dholavira in Kutch, Gujarat, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021, so a Harappan city is now as much a part of India's heritage list as the Taj Mahal.

quiz.q: Why is the Indus valley civilisation also called the Harappan civilisation?
options: Harappa was the first site of this civilisation to be discovered
The word Harappa appears on all its seals
quiz.explain: Archaeologists often name a culture after the first site where it was found. Harappa was the first site discovered.
quiz.mistake: Assumes Harappa was a capital; there is no proof of a capital.

quiz.q: In archaeology, the term 'culture' refers to:
options: A group of objects of a distinctive style found together in a specific area and period
The religion followed by a people
Only the art and music of a people
quiz.explain: An archaeological culture is identified by a set of artefacts of a distinct style that occur together in a region and time.
quiz.mistake: Uses the everyday meaning of culture (art, religion) instead of the archaeological one.

quiz.q: The Mature Harappan civilisation is dated to approximately:
quiz.explain: NCERT dates the Mature Harappan phase to c. 2600–1900 BCE.
quiz.mistake: Picks the Late Harappan or Early Historic period.

quiz.q: Which evidence suggests a break between the Early Harappan and Mature Harappan phases at some sites?
options: Large-scale burning and abandonment of some settlements
Writing changing from right-to-left to left-to-right
quiz.explain: At some sites, burnt layers and abandonment mark a break before the mature phase began.
quiz.mistake: Brings in features (iron, coins) of much later periods.

quiz.q: Which pair of site and present-day location is INCORRECT?
quiz.explain: Kalibangan is in Rajasthan. Shortughai is the Harappan site in Afghanistan.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Kalibangan with Shortughai.

quiz.q: Which of these was a Harappan site located in Afghanistan?
quiz.explain: Shortughai in Afghanistan lay near the source of lapis lazuli. Balakot and Nageshwar are coastal sites; Banawali is in Haryana.
quiz.mistake: Confuses distant trading outposts with coastal sites.

quiz.q: Which statement about Early Harappan cultures is correct?
options: They came after the Mature Harappan cities declined
They had large planned cities like Mohenjodaro
They existed in the same region before the mature phase and had distinctive pottery
quiz.explain: Early Harappan cultures preceded the mature phase; their settlements were generally small, with no large buildings.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'Early' and 'Late' Harappan.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Archaeologists use the term 'Harappan culture' for many sites spread across a large area.
Reason (R): Objects such as seals, beads, weights and baked bricks of a distinctive style are found together at these sites.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The shared set of distinctive artefacts is exactly why the sites are grouped as one culture, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the name comes only from geography, not from shared artefacts.

teach.ask: Gappu flaps in: 'If nobody can read their writing, how do we know all these cities belong to one civilisation?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Shared objects in the same area and time make one culture. Gappu is now an amateur archaeologist!
teach.nudge: Hmm, what kinds of objects do these sites share, and where and when are they found?

learn.hook: A burnt grain of barley, smaller than a grain of rice, can tell us what was cooked in a Mohenjodaro kitchen 4,500 years ago.
points: Harappans ate a wide range of plant and animal products, including fish. Archaeologists reconstruct diet from charred grains and seeds studied by archaeo-botanists.
Grains found include wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame. Millets are found at sites in Gujarat. Finds of rice are relatively rare.
Animal bones include cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig; studies by archaeo-zoologists show these were domesticated.
Bones of wild species such as boar, deer and gharial are also found. We do not know if Harappans hunted these themselves or got the meat from other hunting communities.
Bones of fish and fowl are found as well, so food came from farmers, herders, fisherfolk and possibly hunter-gatherers.

example.q: List the groups that may have supplied food to a Harappan city.
steps: Grains and pulses: farmers.
Milk and meat of cattle, sheep, goat: herders/pastoralists.
Fish: fisherfolk.
Wild animals: hunters, maybe other communities.
example.answer: Peasants, pastoralists, fisherfolk and hunter-gatherers (or communities trading meat).

learn.reallife: Just as Gujarat today grows bajra and jowar while Punjab grows wheat, Harappan millet finds come mainly from Gujarat sites.

quiz.explain: Archaeo-botanists study plant remains; archaeo-zoologists study animal bones.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up plant and animal specialists.

quiz.q: Which grain is relatively RARE among Harappan finds?
quiz.explain: Wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame are common; rice is rare.
quiz.mistake: Projects today's eating habits back onto Harappans.

quiz.q: Finds of millets come mainly from Harappan sites in which region?
quiz.explain: NCERT notes millets are found from sites in Gujarat.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a dry region without recalling the evidence.

quiz.q: Which animals' bones show that the Harappans kept domesticated animals?
options: Cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig
quiz.explain: Bones of cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig indicate domestication.
quiz.mistake: Lists wild species as domesticated.

quiz.q: Why are historians unsure about how Harappans got meat of wild animals like deer and boar?
options: No bones of wild animals have been found
It is unclear whether they hunted themselves or obtained meat from hunting communities
quiz.explain: Wild animal bones are found, but the evidence cannot show who did the hunting.
quiz.mistake: Thinks absence of evidence; in fact the bones exist.

quiz.q: Which of these was NOT among the grains and pulses commonly found at Harappan sites?
quiz.explain: Maize is a New World crop that reached India much later. Lentil, sesame and barley are Harappan finds.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all modern Indian crops existed then.

quiz.q: A case: At a Harappan site, an excavator finds charred barley, fish bones and deer bones in one house. What is the BEST inference?
options: The household was a hunting camp only
The household's food came from varied sources, including farming, fishing and possibly hunting
Barley was grown only for animals
quiz.explain: Mixed remains point to a varied diet drawn from different producers.
quiz.mistake: Over-interprets one type of find and ignores the rest.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Rice was the most common grain at Harappan sites.
Reason (R): Charred grains and seeds help archaeologists reconstruct the Harappan diet.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Rice finds are relatively rare; wheat and barley are common.
quiz.mistake: Projects today's diet back onto the Harappans.

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'How can you know a Harappan's menu if they never wrote recipes?'
teach.praise: Yum! Grains, seeds and bones tell the story. Gappu wants Harappan barley khichdi now!
teach.nudge: Which remains do archaeologists dig up to work out food? Think plants AND animals.

learn.hook: At Kalibangan, archaeologists found a field ploughed nearly 5,000 years ago, with furrows still visible. A farmer in Rajasthan today might recognise the pattern!
points: Seals and terracotta sculptures show the bull was known, so oxen were probably used for ploughing.
Terracotta models of the plough have been found at sites in Cholistan and at Banawali (Haryana).

At Kalibangan (Rajasthan), a ploughed field was found, associated with Early Harappan levels. It had two sets of furrows at right angles to each other, suggesting two different crops were grown together.

Irrigation was probably needed as most Harappan sites lie in semi-arid lands. Traces of canals were found at Shortughai (Afghanistan), but not in Punjab or Sindh. Water from wells and water reservoirs at Dholavira (Gujarat) was also used.
For harvesting, Harappans may have used stone blades set in wooden handles, or metal tools; archaeologists are still not sure.

example.q: Why do furrows at right angles in the Kalibangan field suggest two crops were grown together?
steps: One set of furrows can be used for one crop.
A second set at right angles creates a grid.
Two crops sown in different directions in one field is a known practice.
So the pattern hints at mixed cropping.
example.answer: Criss-crossing furrows suggest that two different crops were grown in the same field at the same time.

learn.reallife: Rajasthan farmers still grow mustard and gram together in one field; the Kalibangan furrows hint that mixed cropping is a very old Indian practice.

quiz.mistake: Assumes the largest cities must have had canals.

The field was used for horse racing
Only one crop was grown each year

quiz.q: Terracotta models of the plough have been found at:
quiz.explain: NCERT mentions terracotta plough models from Cholistan and Banawali.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up evidence for craft and trade sites with farming evidence.

quiz.q: Which site is known for water reservoirs used to store water?
quiz.explain: Dholavira in Gujarat had water reservoirs.
quiz.mistake: Confuses reservoirs with Shortughai's canals.

quiz.q: Why was irrigation probably needed by Harappan farmers?
options: Most Harappan sites are located in semi-arid lands

quiz.mistake: Gives an extreme reason not supported by evidence.

quiz.q: What is the BEST statement about Harappan harvesting tools?
options: They harvested only by hand without tools
They may have used stone blades in wooden handles or metal tools, but this is uncertain
quiz.explain: Archaeologists are unsure; both stone blades and metal tools are possibilities.
quiz.mistake: Assumes iron was available, which belongs to a later period.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Oxen were probably used for ploughing in Harappan times.
Reason (R): The bull appears on seals and in terracotta sculpture.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Familiarity with the bull, shown on seals and terracotta, is the basis for the inference about oxen ploughing.
quiz.mistake: Treats the reason as unrelated evidence.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Did Harappan farmers just throw seeds and pray for rain?'
teach.praise: Super! Ploughs, oxen and water management. Gappu is ready to farm in Kalibangan.
teach.nudge: How did they break the soil, and how did they get water to the fields?

topics.title: Mohenjodaro: a planned city and its drains

learn.hook: Many Indian cities still struggle with waterlogged streets in the monsoon. Mohenjodaro had covered street drains about 4,500 years ago!
points: Mohenjodaro was divided into two parts: a smaller but higher Citadel (to the west) and a much larger but lower Lower Town (to the east). The Citadel was walled, and so was the Lower Town.
Buildings were built on platforms, which served as foundations. This means the settlement was planned first and then built. Platforms needed an enormous amount of labour.
Bricks, sun-dried or baked, were of a standardised ratio: length four times the height and breadth twice the height (4:2:1). This ratio was used across Harappan settlements.
Streets were laid out in an approximately grid pattern, intersecting at right angles. Drains seem to have been laid out first, and houses built along them.
House drains, carrying waste water, were connected to street drains. Long drainage channels had sumps at intervals for cleaning. Drainage systems are found in smaller settlements too, such as Lothal.

example.q: A Harappan brick is 10 cm high. Using the standard ratio, what are its breadth and length?
steps: Ratio length : breadth : height = 4 : 2 : 1.
Breadth = 2 × 10 = 20 cm.
Length = 4 × 10 = 40 cm.

learn.reallife: Smart City projects in India stress planned drainage first. Mohenjodaro's planners seem to have done that long ago: drains first, houses next.

items.text: The Citadel was smaller but ___ than the Lower Town.
Streets were laid in an approximate ___ pattern.

quiz.q: Mohenjodaro was divided into:
options: A larger, higher Citadel and a smaller, lower Lower Town
A smaller, higher Citadel and a larger, lower Lower Town
A temple town and a port
quiz.explain: The Citadel was smaller but higher; the Lower Town was larger but lower.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the size and height of the two parts.

quiz.q: Why does building on platforms suggest that Mohenjodaro was planned?
options: Platforms were made after houses fell down
Platforms show the city grew randomly
The platforms had to be laid first, so the settlement was planned before construction
Platforms were used only for temples
quiz.explain: Platforms acted as foundations; laying them first means the layout was decided in advance.
quiz.mistake: Reverses cause and effect.

quiz.q: A Harappan brick is 12 cm high. What is its length according to the standard ratio?
quiz.explain: Length = 4 × height = 4 × 12 = 48 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the breadth multiplier (2) instead of the length multiplier (4).
steps: Length : height = 4 : 1
Length = 4 × 12 = 48 cm

quiz.q: A Harappan brick has a length of 28 cm. What is its breadth?
quiz.explain: Breadth is half the length (4:2), so 28 ÷ 2 = 14 cm.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 4 and gets the height instead of the breadth.
steps: Length : breadth = 4 : 2 = 2 : 1
Breadth = 28 ÷ 2 = 14 cm

quiz.q: Which feature of Harappan drains made cleaning possible?
options: Drains were open pits inside houses
Drains emptied into the Great Bath
Long channels had sumps at intervals
quiz.explain: Sumps at intervals allowed drains to be cleaned.
quiz.mistake: Imagines drains without any maintenance feature.

quiz.q: Which statement about Harappan drainage is correct?
options: It seems drains were laid out first and houses built along them
Each house threw waste water into the street
Drains were found only at Mohenjodaro
quiz.explain: Planning drains first is suggested; drains are also found in smaller towns like Lothal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks drainage was limited to one city.

quiz.q: Reading a site plan of Mohenjodaro, where would you look for the Great Bath?
quiz.explain: The Great Bath and the warehouse are in the Citadel.
quiz.mistake: Assumes public buildings were in the bigger Lower Town.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Harappan bricks of the same ratio were used at sites far apart.
Reason (R): Brick sizes depended on each family's choice.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true: the 4:2:1 ratio is found across settlements. R is false: standardisation points to common planning, not family choice.
quiz.mistake: Fails to see that standard bricks rule out individual choice.

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'Was Mohenjodaro just a jumble of mud houses?'
teach.praise: Wow, a planned city with drains! Gappu salutes the Harappan town planners.
teach.nudge: What about the two parts of the city, the bricks, and the drains?

topics.title: Houses, the Citadel and the Great Bath

learn.hook: Imagine a house in Mohenjodaro: you walk in from a lane but cannot see the courtyard from the doorway. Privacy mattered even 4,500 years ago!
points: Many Lower Town houses were centred on a courtyard with rooms on all sides. The courtyard was probably used for cooking and weaving, especially in hot and dry weather.
There were no windows in walls along the ground level, and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or the courtyard, which suggests concern for privacy.

Every house had its own bathroom paved with bricks, with drains connected through the wall to the street drains. Some houses had staircases to a second storey or roof. Many houses had wells; Mohenjodaro had about 700 wells.
The Citadel had structures probably used for special public purposes, like the warehouse (only lower brick portions survive; upper wooden parts decayed) and the Great Bath.

The Great Bath was a large rectangular tank in a courtyard with a corridor on all four sides, two flights of steps on the north and south, bricks set on edge with gypsum mortar to make it watertight. Its uniqueness and location suggest a special ritual bath.

example.q: Give two reasons why scholars think the Great Bath had a special, perhaps ritual, purpose.
steps: It is a unique structure, not found elsewhere in that form.
It stands in the Citadel, among public buildings.
It had careful watertight construction and side rooms, one with a large well.
example.answer: Its unique design and its location in the Citadel with other special buildings suggest a ritual bath.

learn.reallife: The idea of a sacred tank survives across India, from temple tanks (kalyani or pushkarini) in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu to ghats on the Ganga.

options: The lower parts were brick; the upper parts were of wood and decayed

quiz.explain: Two flights of steps on the north and south led into the tank.

quiz.q: What was probably the main use of the courtyard in a Harappan house?

quiz.explain: Archaeologists suggest courtyards were used for cooking and weaving.
quiz.mistake: Assigns a public function to a private space.

quiz.q: A case: Across a lane to the north of the Great Bath was a smaller building with eight bathrooms, four on each side of a corridor. What does this suggest?
options: Bathing was organised and may have had a special purpose linked to the Great Bath
Each family in the city had a room there
quiz.explain: Its closeness to the Great Bath and its many bathrooms suggest organised, possibly ritual, bathing.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the building's relation to the Great Bath.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The Great Bath is believed to have been used for some kind of special ritual bath.
Reason (R): It was a distinctive structure located in the Citadel along with other special public buildings.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Its uniqueness and location in the Citadel are the grounds for the ritual interpretation, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the location gives no clue about function.

teach.ask: Gappu is curious: 'What was so special about the houses and the Great Bath?'
teach.praise: Perfect! Courtyard homes, privacy, bathrooms and a ritual bath. Gappu wants a dip!
teach.nudge: Tell Gappu about house design and the special building in the Citadel.

learn.hook: In Egypt, pharaohs were buried with mountains of gold. What did Harappans place in their graves, and what does that tell us?
points: Archaeologists study burials and artefacts to find social or economic differences.

At Harappan burial sites the dead were generally laid in pits. Some pits were lined with bricks. Some graves contain pottery and ornaments, perhaps showing a belief that these could be used in the afterlife.

Jewellery is found in burials of both men and women. In one Harappa burial (excavated in the 1980s), a man had an ornament of three shell rings, a jasper bead and hundreds of micro beads. Some burials had copper mirrors.
Overall, Harappans do not seem to have believed in burying precious things with the dead, so burial differences are not very sharp.

Artefacts are classified as utilitarian (daily-use objects like querns, pottery, needles, flesh-rubbers, made of stone or clay, found everywhere) or luxuries (rare objects of costly non-local materials or complicated technology, such as little faience pots). Faience vessels are found in large cities like Mohenjodaro and Harappa but not in small ones like Kalibangan. Gold was rare and found in hoards.

example.q: A grave has a brick-lined pit with pottery, while another has a plain pit with nothing. What can a historian infer, and what caution is needed?
steps: Brick lining and goods mean more effort and resources.
This hints at differences in status.
But Harappan graves rarely have precious items.
So differences existed but were not extreme.
example.answer: There were some social differences, but the evidence does not show sharp inequality like that in Egyptian royal burials.

learn.reallife: Today, archaeologists at Rakhigarhi in Haryana study skeletons and grave goods with DNA and dating methods to learn about the people buried there.

options: Rare and made from costly, non-local materials or with complicated technology

quiz.explain: A quern for grinding grain is a daily-use object; the others are rare or costly.
quiz.mistake: Confuses rarity with usefulness.

quiz.q: Where are expensive faience vessels mainly found?
options: In large settlements like Mohenjodaro and Harappa
quiz.explain: They are found in large cities and not in small settlements like Kalibangan.
quiz.mistake: Assumes luxuries were evenly spread.

quiz.q: What does the presence of pottery and ornaments in some graves possibly indicate?
options: A belief that these could be used in the afterlife
That the dead were craftsmen only
That burials were done by Mesopotamians
quiz.explain: Grave goods may reflect beliefs about life after death.
quiz.mistake: Reads grave goods as accidental.

quiz.q: What is the overall conclusion about burials as evidence of inequality among Harappans?
options: Burials prove a rich priestly class ruled
Differences existed but were not sharp, as precious things were rarely buried
quiz.explain: Variation exists (brick-lined pits, some goods) but Harappans did not bury great riches.
quiz.mistake: Goes to an extreme in either direction.

quiz.q: Gold among Harappans was:
options: Rare and found in hoards, so it was precious
quiz.explain: Gold was rare and, like today, valued; it is found mostly in hoards.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gold was common or unknown.

quiz.q: In a burial at Harappa, a man was found with an ornament of three shell rings, a jasper bead and hundreds of micro beads. What does this tell us?
options: The man was a Mesopotamian trader
Ornaments were buried with men as well as women
quiz.explain: This burial shows men too were buried with jewellery.
quiz.mistake: Assumes jewellery was only for women.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Faience pots are considered luxury items.
Reason (R): Faience was difficult to make, and such pots are found mainly in large cities.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Difficult technology and limited distribution are exactly why faience pots are classed as luxuries.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the reason to the classification.

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'How can a pot or a grave tell you who was rich?'
teach.praise: Sharp thinking! Burials and luxury objects reveal differences. Gappu is impressed.
teach.nudge: Which two kinds of evidence help trace social differences?

learn.hook: A red carnelian bead from the Indus could end up in a royal grave in Mesopotamia. Its journey began at a tiny town called Chanhudaro.
points: Chanhudaro was a tiny settlement (less than 7 hectares) almost exclusively devoted to craft production: bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making.
Bead materials: stones like carnelian (beautiful red), jasper, crystal, quartz and steatite; metals like copper, bronze and gold; and shell, faience and terracotta (burnt clay).
Beads were made in many shapes: disc, cylindrical, spherical, barrel and segmented. Some were decorated by incising or painting, some had etched designs.

Techniques: nodules were chipped into rough shapes, then flaked into final form; grinding, polishing and drilling completed the process. The red colour of carnelian came from firing the yellowish raw material and beads at various stages. Specialised drills have been found at Chanhudaro, Lothal and Dholavira.

To identify a production centre, archaeologists look for raw material (stone nodules, whole shells, copper ore), tools, unfinished objects, rejects and waste material. Waste is one of the best indicators.

example.q: An excavator finds shell pieces with cut marks, broken bangles and whole shells in one area. Is it a craft workshop?
steps: Whole shells = raw material.
Pieces with cut marks = waste.
Broken bangles = rejects/unfinished objects.
All three together point to production on the spot.
example.answer: Yes, it was probably a shell-working centre, because raw material, waste and unfinished objects are found together.

learn.reallife: Khambhat (Cambay) in Gujarat is still famous for agate and carnelian bead-making, a craft with roots going back to Harappan times.

games.title: How a carnelian bead was made

Grind, polish and drill

quiz.q: Chanhudaro is known as a settlement:

Almost exclusively devoted to craft production
quiz.explain: Chanhudaro was a small site focused on crafts such as bead-making and seal-making.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Chanhudaro with Mohenjodaro or Kalibangan.

quiz.q: How was the red colour of carnelian beads obtained?
options: By firing the yellowish raw material and beads at various stages
By painting them with red ochre
By mixing copper into the stone
quiz.explain: Heating changes the yellowish stone to red.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the colour was painted on.

quiz.explain: Waste and unfinished items show manufacture took place there.

quiz.explain: NCERT lists all five crafts at Chanhudaro.
quiz.mistake: Picks a single craft or anachronistic iron-working.

quiz.q: Which material was NOT used to make Harappan beads?
quiz.explain: Harappans used faience, a glass-like paste, but not true glass. Carnelian and steatite were major bead materials.
quiz.mistake: Confuses faience with glass.

quiz.q: Specialised drills for bead-making have been found at:
quiz.explain: Drills come from Chanhudaro, Lothal and, more recently, Dholavira.
quiz.mistake: Guesses big cities rather than recalling craft sites.

quiz.q: What is the correct sequence for shaping a stone bead?
options: Chip into rough shape → flake into final form → grind, polish and drill
quiz.explain: Rough chipping comes first, then fine flaking, then finishing.
quiz.mistake: Places finishing steps before shaping.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Archaeologists use waste material to identify craft production centres.
Reason (R): Waste shows that raw material was worked at that place.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Leftover waste is direct evidence of work done on site, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks waste is just rubbish with no information.

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'How do you know beads were made in Chanhudaro and not just bought there?'
teach.praise: Excellent detective work! Gappu now wants a carnelian bead necklace.
teach.nudge: What would you find at a workshop that you wouldn't find in a shop?

learn.hook: Copper from Rajasthan, gold from the south, blue lapis lazuli from Afghanistan: Harappan craftspeople ran a supply chain long before trucks and railways.
points: Harappans got raw materials in many ways. Bullock carts carried goods over land; riverine routes along the Indus and its tributaries and coastal routes were probably also used. Terracotta toy models of bullock carts have been found.

One strategy was to set up settlements near sources: Nageshwar and Balakot near shell sources; Shortughai in far Afghanistan near lapis lazuli (a blue stone); Lothal near carnelian (from Bharuch, Gujarat), steatite (south Rajasthan and north Gujarat) and metal (Rajasthan).
Nageshwar and Balakot specialised in making shell objects such as bangles, ladles and inlay, which were sent to other settlements.
Another strategy was sending expeditions: to the Khetri region of Rajasthan for copper and to South India for gold.

In the Khetri area, archaeologists found evidence of the Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture, with distinctive non-Harappan pottery and an unusual wealth of copper objects. Its people may have supplied copper to the Harappans.

example.q: Why would the Harappans set up Shortughai so far away in Afghanistan?
steps: Shortughai lies near sources of lapis lazuli.
Lapis lazuli was a highly valued blue stone.
A settlement near the source made regular supply easier.
example.answer: To secure a steady supply of lapis lazuli from close to its source.

learn.reallife: Today, India's Khetri Copper Complex in Rajasthan (Hindustan Copper Ltd) works the same copper belt that Harappans may have obtained copper from.

items.text: Shell bangles, ladles and inlay were made at Nageshwar and ___.

quiz.q: The Khetri region of Rajasthan was an important source of:
quiz.explain: Expeditions went to Khetri for copper.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Khetri copper with South Indian gold.

quiz.q: Harappans obtained gold mainly through expeditions to:
quiz.explain: NCERT mentions expeditions to South India for gold.
quiz.mistake: Confuses gold with copper sources.

quiz.q: Which culture in the Khetri area had distinctive non-Harappan pottery and an unusual wealth of copper objects?
quiz.explain: The Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture may have supplied copper to Harappans.
quiz.mistake: Recalls later cultures unrelated to Harappan trade.

quiz.q: Which pair of settlement and raw material is correctly matched?
quiz.explain: Shortughai was near lapis lazuli. Nageshwar and Balakot were shell centres; Khetri gave copper.
quiz.mistake: Shuffles the sources.

quiz.q: Lothal was located near sources of:
quiz.explain: Lothal was near carnelian (Bharuch), steatite and metal sources.
quiz.mistake: Picks Shortughai's lapis lazuli.

quiz.q: Which objects were made at Nageshwar and Balakot?
quiz.explain: These coastal sites specialised in shell objects.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the coastal location links them to shell.

quiz.q: What does a terracotta toy model of a bullock cart suggest?
options: Children were taught to drive carts
Carts were used only in rituals
Bullock carts were an important means of overland transport
quiz.explain: Such models, plus the needs of trade, suggest overland transport by bullock carts.
quiz.mistake: Overlooks the transport role.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Harappans set up a settlement at Shortughai.
Reason (R): Shortughai lay near the copper mines of Khetri.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Shortughai, in Afghanistan, was near lapis lazuli sources; Khetri copper is in Rajasthan.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the sources of lapis lazuli and copper.

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: 'Where did Harappans get copper and gold if their cities didn't have mines?'
teach.praise: Great! Settlements near sources plus expeditions. Gappu is now a logistics manager.
teach.nudge: Name the two strategies and a few sources for materials.

learn.hook: Clay tablets from Mesopotamia speak of a far-off land called Meluhha that sent carnelian and timber. Many scholars think that land was the Harappan region!
points: Copper was probably brought from Oman, on the southeastern tip of the Arabian peninsula. Chemical analyses show both Omani copper and Harappan artefacts have traces of nickel, suggesting a common origin.
A large Harappan jar coated with a thick layer of black clay has been found at Omani sites, and Harappan objects have been found there too.
Mesopotamian texts from about the mid-third millennium BCE mention contact with Dilmun (probably the island of Bahrain), Magan (perhaps Oman) and Meluhha (possibly the Harappan region).

Products from Meluhha mentioned include carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold and varieties of wood. A Mesopotamian myth says of Meluhha: 'May your bird be the haja-bird' — some scholars think the haja-bird was the peacock.
Meluhha is described as a land of seafarers. Mesopotamian seals show ships and boats, and Persian Gulf seals have been found, suggesting sea trade.

example.q: A Mesopotamian text lists carnelian and timber coming from 'Meluhha'. Why do scholars identify Meluhha with the Harappan region?
steps: The goods listed (carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold, wood) match Harappan resources.
Harappan objects and seals are found in the Gulf region.
Meluhha is called a land of seafarers, fitting coastal Harappan sites.
example.answer: Because the goods and the evidence of sea links match the Harappan region, though the identification is still 'possible', not certain.

learn.reallife: Gujarat's Lothal is being developed as a National Maritime Heritage Complex, recalling India's earliest sea trade with the Gulf.

quiz.explain: A shared trace element points to a common source for the copper.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the direction of trade.

quiz.explain: Magan is perhaps Oman; Dilmun is probably Bahrain; Meluhha possibly the Harappan region.

quiz.mistake: Picks goods of other times and regions.

quiz.explain: The haja-bird has been suggested to be the peacock.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a common bird.

quiz.q: Which evidence points to sea trade between the Harappans and the Gulf region?

quiz.mistake: Assumes coins existed in Harappan times.

quiz.explain: Dilmun is probably Bahrain in the Persian Gulf.
quiz.mistake: Guesses an island near India.

quiz.q:

Reason (R): Meluhha is described as a land of seafarers and as the source of carnelian, lapis lazuli and timber.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The described goods and seafaring match the Harappan region; this is the basis of the identification.
quiz.mistake: Treats the reason as unrelated.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Did Harappans ever travel beyond India?'
teach.praise: Bon voyage! Gappu is sailing to Dilmun with a bag of carnelian beads.
teach.nudge: What do Mesopotamian texts and Omani finds tell us?

learn.hook: Your online parcel has a barcode; a Harappan sack of goods had a clay sealing. Both said: 'Untouched, from the right sender!'
points: Seals and sealings were used to facilitate long-distance communication. A sack of goods was tied with rope, the knot covered with wet clay, and seals pressed on it. The impression is called a sealing; an intact sealing showed the goods were not tampered with and identified the sender.
The Harappan seal is typically made of steatite (a stone). It often has an animal motif and signs from a script that remains undeciphered.
The script was probably not alphabetic, because it has too many signs: somewhere between 375 and 400. It was written from right to left (wider spacing on the right, cramped on the left).
Inscriptions are short; the longest has about 26 signs. Writing appears on seals, copper tools, rims of jars, copper and terracotta tablets, jewellery, bone rods and even an ancient signboard.

Weights were usually cubical, made of chert, with no markings. Lower denominations were binary (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, … up to 12,800), while higher denominations followed the decimal system. Smaller weights were probably for jewellery and beads; metal scale-pans have been found.

example.q: In the binary series 1, 2, 4, 8, …, what are the next three weights after 8?
steps: Each weight is double the previous one.

learn.reallife: Courier companies and India Post use tamper-proof seals and tracking codes; Harappan sealings did the same job of proving goods were untouched.

quiz.mistake: Assumes Harappans used coins or land grants, which belong to later periods.

quiz.q: Harappan seals were usually made of:
quiz.explain: The typical Harappan seal is made of steatite.

options: It has too many signs, between 375 and 400
quiz.explain: An alphabet has a small number of signs; 375–400 is far too many.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the length of the longest inscription (26 signs) with the number of signs.

quiz.q: How do we know the Harappan script was written from right to left?
options: Some seals show wider spacing on the right and cramped signs on the left
quiz.explain: The writer began on the right with room to spare and ran out of space on the left.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the script has been read.

quiz.explain: Lower denominations were binary, doubling each time; higher ones were decimal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all weights were decimal.

quiz.explain: Doubling 32 gives 64.

Smaller ones were probably used for jewellery and beads
They carried inscribed numbers on every face
quiz.explain: Harappan weights had no markings.
quiz.mistake: Assumes weights must be labelled to be used.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The Harappan script has been deciphered with the help of a bilingual inscription.
Reason (R): The Harappan script was written from right to left.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The script is still undeciphered; its right-to-left direction is known from the spacing of signs.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Harappan script with Brahmi or Kharosthi.

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'If no one can read the script, what can we still learn from seals and weights?'
teach.praise: Fantastic! Seals secured trade and weights kept it fair. Gappu weighs his seeds in binary now.
teach.nudge: What were seals used for, and what was special about the script and weights?

topics.title: Ancient authority: who ruled the Harappans?

learn.hook: Same brick ratio from Punjab to Gujarat, same weights, planned cities. Who made all these decisions? Historians still argue!
points: Signs of complex decisions: extraordinary uniformity of Harappan artefacts (pottery, seals, weights, bricks); bricks of standard ratio even though not produced in a single centre; planned settlements; craft production organised in places near raw materials.
Palace and king? A large building at Mohenjodaro was labelled a palace by archaeologists, but no spectacular finds were associated with it.

A stone statue was labelled 'priest-king' because archaeologists were familiar with Mesopotamian history and its 'priest-kings'. Harappan ritual practices are not yet understood, so we cannot know if those who performed them held political power.

Theories: (1) there were no rulers and everybody enjoyed equal status; (2) there was no single ruler but several, such as one each for Mohenjodaro and Harappa; (3) these were part of a single state, given the similarity in artefacts, planned settlements, standard bricks and settlements near raw material sources.
As things stand, the last theory seems the most plausible, as it is unlikely entire communities could have collectively made and implemented such complex decisions.

example.q: Which theory of Harappan political organisation does the uniformity of bricks across distant sites support most strongly, and why?
steps: Bricks were made in many places, not in one factory.
Yet they share the same 4:2:1 ratio.
Such uniformity suggests decisions taken and enforced over a large area.
This fits best with a single state.
example.answer: It supports the single-state theory, since a common authority could enforce such standards.

learn.reallife: The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) sets uniform standards for bricks, cement and more across India today; Harappan standardisation suggests some authority did a similar job.

quiz.explain: The uniformity and planning point to some central authority.
quiz.mistake: Invents evidence like palaces or inscriptions.

No spectacular finds were associated with it

quiz.mistake: Misses the significance of decentralised yet uniform production.

options: Harappan ritual practices are not yet understood
quiz.explain: Without understanding the rituals, we cannot know whether those performing them also ruled.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the evidence is clear one way or the other.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The label 'priest-king' does not prove that Harappan priests were also rulers.
Reason (R): The label was borrowed from Mesopotamian history, and Harappan ritual practices are not yet understood.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Because the label comes from Mesopotamia and Harappan rituals are not understood, the statue cannot prove priestly rule. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Treats a modern label as ancient evidence.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'So who was the boss of the Harappans?'
teach.praise: Well argued! Three theories, and the single state seems most plausible. Gappu is now a historian.
teach.nudge: Can you give the different theories and the evidence for the most plausible one?

learn.hook: Imagine a city where people stopped using writing, seals and standard weights within a few generations. That is roughly what happened after c. 1900 BCE.
points: By c. 1800 BCE most Mature Harappan sites in regions such as Cholistan had been abandoned.
At the same time, population expanded into new settlements in Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

In the few Harappan sites that continued to be occupied after 1900 BCE, material culture changed: distinctive artefacts such as weights, seals and special beads disappeared; writing, long-distance trade and craft specialisation also disappeared. House construction techniques deteriorated and large public structures were no longer built. These are called Late Harappan or 'successor' cultures, and show a rural way of life.
Suggested causes include climatic change, deforestation, excessive floods, the shifting and/or drying up of rivers, and overuse of the landscape.

These causes may explain the end of some settlements but not the collapse of a whole civilisation. One explanation is the disappearance of a strong unifying element, perhaps the Harappan state, shown by the vanishing of seals, the script, distinctive beads and pottery.

example.q: Why is 'floods' alone not a convincing explanation for the end of the entire Harappan civilisation?
steps: Floods could ruin settlements near rivers.
But Harappan sites were spread over a vast area with different conditions.
A local cause cannot explain the simultaneous disappearance of seals, script and weights everywhere.
So a wider explanation, like the collapse of a unifying state, is suggested.
example.answer: Floods may explain the abandonment of some sites but not the civilisation-wide loss of seals, script and standard weights.

learn.reallife: Ghaggar-Hakra channels and drying rivers are studied by Indian scientists today using satellite images from ISRO to understand how river shifts affected ancient settlements.

quiz.q:

Reason (R): Such causes may account for the decline of some settlements but not the collapse of the whole civilisation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Local causes do not explain a civilisation-wide collapse; R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Believes a single local cause is enough.

teach.ask: Gappu sighs: 'Why did such great cities just fade away?'
teach.praise: Clear and balanced! Many causes, plus the end of a unifying state. Gappu nods wisely.
teach.nudge: What changed in material culture, and what causes have been suggested?

learn.hook: Alexander Cunningham held a Harappan seal in his hands in the 1870s but could not tell how old it was. The discovery waited another 50 years!
points: Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), began excavations in the mid-nineteenth century. He used accounts of Chinese Buddhist pilgrims (4th–7th centuries CE) to locate early settlements; his main interest was the Early Historic period.
Harappa did not fit his framework. An Englishman gave him a Harappan seal; he tried to place it in a familiar time-frame and failed to realise how old Harappa was (Report on Harappan seal, 1875).

In the early twentieth century, Daya Ram Sahni found seals at Harappa in layers much older than Early Historic levels; R.D. Banerji found similar seals at Mohenjodaro. In 1924 John Marshall, Director-General of the ASI, announced the discovery of a new civilisation in the Indus valley.

Marshall excavated along regular horizontal units measured uniformly throughout the mound, ignoring the site's stratigraphy. So artefacts from different layers were grouped together and their context was lost.

R.E.M. Wheeler, Director-General of the ASI from 1944, corrected this by following the stratigraphy of the mound. Later landmarks: Wheeler at Harappa (1946), S.R. Rao at Lothal (1955), B.B. Lal and B.K. Thapar at Kalibangan (1960), R.S. Bisht at Dholavira (1990).

example.q: Why was Marshall's method a problem?
steps: A mound has layers formed at different times (stratigraphy).
Marshall dug in uniform horizontal units regardless of layers.
Objects from different layers got mixed in one unit.
So their date and context were lost.
example.answer: Ignoring stratigraphy mixed up artefacts of different periods, destroying valuable information about context.

learn.reallife: The ASI, founded in Cunningham's time, still protects over 3,600 monuments across India, from Dholavira to the Red Fort.

quiz.q: Who was the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India?
quiz.explain: Cunningham was the first DG of the ASI.
quiz.mistake: Confuses him with Marshall, a later DG.

quiz.q: Cunningham used the accounts of which travellers to locate early settlements?
quiz.explain: He relied on Chinese Buddhist pilgrims who visited between the 4th and 7th centuries CE.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Megasthenes or later travellers.

quiz.q: Why did Cunningham fail to recognise the importance of Harappa?
options: He could read the Harappan script but disliked it
Harappan objects did not fit his framework of Early Historic Indian history
quiz.explain: He tried to place Harappan finds in the Early Historic period he knew, and could not.
quiz.mistake: Thinks he lacked access rather than the right framework.

quiz.q: In which year did John Marshall announce the discovery of a new civilisation in the Indus valley?
quiz.explain: Marshall made the announcement in 1924.
quiz.mistake: Picks Cunningham's report (1875) or Wheeler's work (1946).

quiz.q: Who found seals at Mohenjodaro similar to those at Harappa?
quiz.explain: R.D. Banerji found seals at Mohenjodaro; Daya Ram Sahni found them at Harappa.
quiz.mistake: Swaps Banerji and Sahni.

quiz.q: What was the main problem with Marshall's excavation method?
options: He dug in uniform horizontal units and ignored stratigraphy
quiz.explain: Ignoring layers meant artefacts from different periods were grouped together.
quiz.mistake: Misses the core issue of stratigraphy.

quiz.q: Which archaeologist began excavations at Dholavira in 1990?
quiz.explain: R.S. Bisht began excavating Dholavira in 1990.
quiz.mistake: Links Dholavira to the wrong archaeologist.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): John Marshall announced the discovery of a new civilisation in 1924.
Reason (R): Marshall carefully followed the stratigraphy of the mound.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Marshall ignored stratigraphy; it was Wheeler who followed it.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the methods of Marshall and Wheeler.

teach.ask: Gappu flutters: 'Who actually discovered the Harappan civilisation?'
teach.praise: Top marks! From Cunningham's confusion to Wheeler's layers. Gappu claps his wings.
teach.nudge: Who found the seals, who announced the civilisation, and how did excavation methods change?

topics.title: New sites and the problems of interpretation

learn.hook: A small clay figure of a woman with heavy jewellery: is she a goddess, a toy or a household charm? Archaeologists must decide with no label attached!
points: After Partition (1947) the major sites Harappa and Mohenjodaro were in Pakistan. Indian archaeologists explored new areas: surveys in Kutch, Punjab and Haryana added many sites, with Kalibangan, Lothal, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira excavated in India. Explorations continued in Pakistan too.

New techniques and questions: scientific analysis of materials, and studies of plant and animal remains, are used to understand diet, trade and environment; since the 1980s there has been growing international interest.

Classifying finds is a basic step: by material (stone, clay, metal, bone, ivory) and by function. Function is hard to know; archaeologists often compare with present-day objects (e.g. querns) or study the context of the find.

Religion is inferred from objects: terracotta female figurines, heavily jewelled with elaborate head-dresses, were called 'mother goddesses'; rare stone statues of men seated in a standard posture were labelled 'priest-king'; fire altars are reported from Kalibangan and Lothal; seals show a 'unicorn' and a figure seated cross-legged in a 'yogic' posture surrounded by animals, regarded as 'proto-Shiva'; conical stones have been classified as lingas.

Such interpretations often use later traditions. For example, Rudra appears in the Rigveda, but he is not depicted there as Pashupati or as a yogi. So using later texts to explain Harappan objects has limits.

example.q: Why is the 'proto-Shiva' identification of the yogic figure on a seal debated?
steps: The identification relies on later Hindu ideas of Shiva as Pashupati and yogi.
The Rigveda, an earlier text, mentions Rudra.
But Rudra in the Rigveda is not shown as Pashupati or as a yogi.
So the link between the seal and later Shiva is uncertain.
example.answer: Because it projects later religious ideas backwards; even the Rigveda's Rudra does not match the image.

learn.reallife: Archaeologists at Rakhigarhi (Haryana) have used ancient DNA analysis, an example of new scientific techniques changing what we know about Harappans.

games.title: Interpretation check
items: Fire altars have been reported from Kalibangan and Lothal.
These are cited as possible ritual evidence.
The Rigveda describes Rudra as a yogi surrounded by animals.
Rudra is not depicted as Pashupati or a yogi in the Rigveda.
Archaeologists sometimes infer an object's function by comparing it with present-day objects.
Querns are an example.
After Partition, Harappa and Mohenjodaro remained in India.
Both went to Pakistan.
Dholavira was excavated in India after Partition.
It lies in Kutch, Gujarat.

quiz.q: After Partition, why did Indian archaeologists explore regions like Kutch, Punjab and Haryana?
options: The major sites Harappa and Mohenjodaro were now in Pakistan
quiz.explain: With the main sites in Pakistan, Indian archaeologists searched for sites within India.
quiz.mistake: Misses the impact of Partition on archaeology.

quiz.q: Which identification has been criticised because it depends on later religious traditions?
quiz.explain: The proto-Shiva label uses later ideas of Shiva to interpret a Harappan image.
quiz.mistake: Picks evidence that is not religious.

quiz.q: Why are some terracotta female figurines called 'mother goddesses'?
options: They were found in temples with priests
They are heavily jewelled with elaborate head-dresses and are thought to be objects of worship
quiz.explain: The label is an interpretation based on their appearance; it is not proven.
quiz.mistake: Believes the label rests on readable inscriptions.

quiz.q: What is the main difficulty in classifying Harappan artefacts by function?
options: Archaeologists must infer use indirectly, by comparison with present-day objects or from context
Every object had only one material
quiz.explain: Function is usually inferred indirectly, which creates uncertainty.
quiz.mistake: Thinks function is obvious from the object.

quiz.q: Fire altars that may suggest ritual practice have been reported at:
quiz.explain: NCERT mentions fire altars at Kalibangan and Lothal.
quiz.mistake: Recalls sites linked with crafts or trade instead.

quiz.q: Which new technique has helped answer questions about Harappan diet and environment?
options: Studies of plant and animal remains
quiz.explain: Archaeo-botany and archaeo-zoology reveal diet and environment.
quiz.mistake: Assumes texts or coins exist.

quiz.q: A case: An excavation report says a stone object was found inside a house next to a hearth, worn smooth on one face. What should an archaeologist do first?
options: Ignore it because it has no inscription
Assume it was imported from Mesopotamia
Use the context and wear pattern, and compare with known objects like querns, before deciding its function
quiz.explain: Context and comparison guide interpretation; jumping to a ritual label is unsafe.
quiz.mistake: Labels unfamiliar objects as religious without evidence.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Using later texts to interpret Harappan religion has limits.
Reason (R): The Rigveda's Rudra is not depicted as Pashupati or a yogi, unlike the 'proto-Shiva' seal.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The mismatch between the earlier text and the seal shows why projecting later traditions backwards is risky.
quiz.mistake: Assumes later traditions always explain earlier objects.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Can we really tell what Harappans worshipped?'
teach.praise: Thoughtful! You showed both the clues and their limits. Gappu is a careful historian now.
teach.nudge: What objects are linked to religion, and why must we be careful with those labels?
